subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: The practice has a distinct, consistent brand mark — a gold monogram "T" logo that appears identically on desktop and mobile — and a genuinely broad treatment menu, cleanly split into "Services" and "We Offer" categories covering hair restoration, joint injections, peptides, IV therapy, testosterone therapy and weight loss. That range is a real asset once a visitor reaches it.

The first screen does not carry that asset forward. On both devices the headline is "TRIED & TRUE MEDSPA" — the business name again, already stated in the logo directly above it — with no line naming a specialty, a location, or what happens next. The only button is a circular "View more" with no stated destination, and no booking, scheduling or phone action appears anywhere in the navigation captured. No provider is named or pictured on the first screen; the one credibility line found ("over 27 years of combined experience") is unattributed to a person.

Evidence limitation: this review is based on a homepage text extract and one screenshot per device (desktop and mobile first screens), all captured previously. No live re-crawl, treatment-page fetch or performance test was run for this report, so the score is normalised across the six categories that could be assessed. No traffic, revenue or review figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). The lowest scores are concentrated in booking and trust — no visible way to book, and no named provider on the first screen — with positioning also weak because the headline repeats the business name rather than saying what the practice does.

scorecard.finding: Headline repeats the logo's business name; no specialty or location stated.
No named provider; only an unattributed "27 years" experience line.
No booking/schedule action found in the navigation or hero on either device.
"View more" gives no indication of what happens next.
Renders cleanly with a good tap target, but offers no next step above the fold.
No city, address or phone number appears on either captured first screen.

strengthsLead: The practice has real substance behind the homepage — it just isn't reaching the first screen yet.

strengths.title: A distinct, consistent brand mark.
strengths.body: The gold monogram "T" logo and "TRIED & TRUE MEDSPA" wordmark appear identically on desktop and mobile, giving the practice a recognisable, upscale visual identity that travels across the site.

strengths.title: A genuinely broad, organised treatment menu.
strengths.body: Hair Restoration, Joint Injections, TNTMS Microneedling, Peptides WL, Regenerative IV Therapy, Testosterone Therapy and Weight Loss are all named and split sensibly between "Services" and "We Offer" rather than dumped into one long list.

strengths.title: The mobile hero is legible with a clear tap target.
strengths.body: White text over a photo background reads cleanly at 390 pixels wide, and the circular "View more" button is a comfortable size to tap — the mechanics are sound even where the messaging is not.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The hero shows a woman measuring her waist with a tape measure behind the headline "TRIED & TRUE MEDSPA" and a circular "View more" button. The navigation reads "FAQ´S" with an acute-accent character in place of an apostrophe, and an unlabeled icon sits at its right end.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. A different carousel slide — a muscular male torso — sits behind the same headline and "View more" button. Beneath it, a teaser reads "Hair Restoration at Tried & True Med Spa" with the line "over 27 years of combined experience in medical aesthetics and hair restoration", unattributed to a named provider.

findings.heading: The headline repeats the business name already shown in the logo.
findings.evidence: On both desktop and mobile, the hero headline reads "TRIED & TRUE MEDSPA" — the same wordmark that sits in the logo directly above it. No supporting line names a specialty, a location, or a reason to choose the practice.
findings.why: A first-time visitor decides within seconds whether a page is relevant to them. Restating the company name teaches them nothing about what is treated, who it suits, or where it is — the three questions a full-fee patient is trying to answer before reading further.
findings.recommended: Replace or supplement the headline with a positioning line naming the primary specialty and the Atlanta location.

findings.heading: No booking, scheduling or call action appears anywhere in what was captured.
findings.evidence: The full navigation (Home, About Us, Services, We Offer, FAQ'S, Contact, Search) contains no "Book" or "Schedule" item. The only buttons visible in the screenshots are a circular "View more" on the hero and a plain "View More" text link under the Hair Restoration teaser — neither states a destination.
findings.why: A patient ready to act should not have to guess. An ambiguous "View more" gives no signal whether it opens a booking form, a service page, or nothing specific at all, and the absence of any scheduling or phone action at this stage is a real point of friction.
findings.recommended: Add a persistently visible "Book a Consultation" (or equivalent) button to the header, distinct from the generic "View more" links.

findings.heading: No provider is named or pictured on the first screen.
findings.evidence: Neither hero image identifies a doctor or provider. The only credibility line found is "over 27 years of combined experience in medical aesthetics and hair restoration", under the Hair Restoration teaser on mobile — attributed to the practice generally, not to a named person.
findings.why: For injectables, hormone therapy and joint injections, the decision a patient is making is about the person delivering care. An unattributed experience claim carries far less weight than a named, credentialed provider would.
findings.recommended: Name and credential the lead provider(s) on the homepage, ideally near the hero or the experience line already in place.

findings.heading: The hero image differs between desktop and mobile and does not clearly signal a medical spa.
findings.evidence: The desktop hero shows a woman measuring her waist with a tape measure; the mobile hero — a different carousel slide — shows a muscular male torso. Neither image is captioned or otherwise tied to a specific treatment.
findings.why: Without an explanation, a visitor has to guess whether this is a weight-loss clinic, a fitness brand, or a medical spa, adding effort before the headline itself has said anything concrete.
findings.recommended: Use imagery of the clinic, team or a captioned treatment photo that stays consistent across breakpoints.

findings.heading: A typo and an unlabeled icon sit in the main navigation.
findings.evidence: The desktop navigation reads "FAQ´S", using an acute-accent character in place of an apostrophe. Immediately to its right is a short underlined icon with no text label and no stated destination.
findings.why: Small as it is, a visible typo in the primary navigation of a medical practice works against the impression of care and attention a prospective full-fee patient is unconsciously scanning for.
findings.recommended: Correct the punctuation to "FAQ's" and either label the unlabeled icon or remove it.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: The navigation mostly follows convention (Home, About, Services, Contact), but an unlabeled icon and an ambiguous "View more" button sit outside what visitors expect to find.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: The "View more" circle is a comfortable tap target on mobile, but no booking or call action is offered at comparable prominence on either device.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: The one credibility line — "27 years of combined experience" — sits below the hero on mobile, not next to any action button, and is absent from the desktop first screen.
No named provider appears on either first screen captured — the weakest category in this review.
"View more" does not say what it leads to, and no booking, scheduling or phone action is offered above the fold on either device.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: None observed — no free-consultation offer, featured treatment, or similar default appears on the first screen.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: What text is visible is plain and unembellished ("over 27 years of combined experience"), without overclaiming — though there is little content yet to assess this against.

roadmap.actions: Correct "FAQ´S" to "FAQ's" and label or remove the unlabeled navigation icon. Add a "Book a Consultation" button to the header. Add a specialty and location line beneath the existing headline.

Name and credential the lead provider(s) near the hero or the existing experience line. Replace or caption the hero imagery so it matches the stated services, and keep the same hero content across desktop and mobile.

Add a rating and review count where publicly available. Review treatment-page depth and technical performance, which were outside the scope of this homepage review. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become the practice's own.

limitations: This review is based on a homepage text extract and two screenshots (desktop and mobile first screens) already on file; no live re-crawl, treatment-page fetch or performance test was carried out for this report. The booking path, any phone number and any address were not traced beyond what appears in the captured evidence, so their absence here means absent from what was captured, not necessarily absent from the site as a whole. Treatment content and technical/performance are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available).
